title: Fisheries of the Exclusive Economic Zone Off Alaska; Pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the Gulf of Alaska
summary:
Two federal moves stood out in today’s Federal Register: a policy from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau about what can appear in credit reports, and a temporary closure of a pollock fishery in the Gulf of Alaska to avoid exceeding harvest limits.

On credit reporting, the Bureau issued guidance saying federal law limits states’ ability to decide which types of information can show up on consumer reports, including categories like medical debt or arrest records. The agency argues that letting each state set its own rules would create a patchwork that makes credit reports less comparable across the country, could raise borrowing costs, and might force lenders to price loans differently depending on where people live. The guidance also criticizes a 2022 view that states could block whole categories of information, calling that approach inconsistent with how federal law regulates how long negative items can stay on reports. This is guidance only—it doesn’t carry the force of law—but it signals how the Bureau interprets the rules and how it may act going forward.

Who benefits? National lenders and credit reporting companies get a clearer, more uniform playbook, which may make underwriting simpler and keep borrowing standards consistent across state lines. Consumers with strong credit histories could benefit if lenders feel more confident in the data they use. Who might be negatively affected? States aiming to limit the reporting of sensitive items like medical debt may see their efforts curtailed, and consumers burdened by such debt could lose protections that some state laws have been pursuing.

In the Gulf of Alaska, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration closed directed fishing for pollock in one management area after determining the yearly catch limit has been or will be reached. The closure runs from October 25 through the end of 2025, with a small amount set aside for incidental catch to support other fisheries. This move is intended to protect the stock and keep the fishery within science-based limits.

Who benefits? The pollock population, the broader ecosystem, and the long-term health of the fishery. Who might be negatively affected? Fishing vessels, processors, and coastal communities that rely on late-season pollock may face short-term economic hits, and buyers could see tighter supply. The agency skipped a longer comment period to act quickly, citing fresh catch data and the need to prevent an overrun.
